title: the blessing before eating
hookLine: the blessing before eating; saying thank you to the source

cards: Watch someone who keeps this tradition pick up an apple. Before the first bite there's a pause, about two seconds long, and a murmur you'd miss if you weren't looking. Then the bite.
Same with a glass of water. A cookie. A piece of bread at a wedding.
A lot of eating happens the way scrolling does: mid-sentence, standing up, already on to the next thing. This is the opposite. A tiny speed bump between wanting something and having it.
And the words inside that pause have a surprising reason behind them. Today: the two-second blessing.

teach.b: A bracha is a blessing. The standard form opens with the same words each time: baruch atah Adonai, eloheinu melech ha-olam, roughly, blessed are you, Lord our God, ruler of the world.
Then the ending changes with the food. For bread: who brings forth bread from the earth. For fruit: who creates the fruit of the tree.
For water, or almost anything else: by whose word all things came to be. Here's the surprise. It's not the food being blessed.
The blessing is said to the source of the food. Why bother? The rabbis noticed two psalms that seem to disagree.
One says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof."

teach.h: BUT THE EARTH HATH HE GIVEN.
teach.b: Another says: "The heavens are the heavens of the LORD; but the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it? Does the world belong to God, or to us?
Their answer: both, and the blessing is the hinge. Before the blessing, the apple is still God's. After it, it's been given to you.
To eat without a blessing, they said, is a little like taking something that isn't yours yet.

There's a blessing after eating too, and the Torah puts it in the order people actually eat: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God." First eat, then be full, then say thanks.
One rabbi, Rabbi Meir, taught that a person should say a hundred blessings every day.
It sounds like a lot until you count how many things in a day get done without a second look. A hundred small pauses.

how: Observant Jews say a short blessing before eating or drinking, with a different ending for bread, fruit, vegetables, wine and other foods, and a longer grace after meals, the Birkat Hamazon, after eating bread.

games.q: what's inside the blessing — tap the pairs.
p: who brings forth bread from the earth

s: the blessing is said over the food to make it holy
it's said to the source of the food, not to the food.
there's a blessing after eating as well as before
"thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless": grace after meals.
the rabbis found two psalms that seem to disagree about who owns the earth
one says the earth is the LORD's; one says it's given to people. the blessing is the hinge.

games.q: one psalm says the earth is God's. another says God gave the earth to people. you're one of the rabbis. how do you square them?
o: before a blessing it's God's; after, it's given to you.
the earth is God's, the sky is ours.
games.why: the rabbis' answer: before the blessing everything is still God's; the blessing is how it's handed to you.

practice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. If there's something to eat or drink near you, hold it, even a glass of water. Look at it.
Think of the hands it passed through to reach you: a farmer, a driver, someone stocking a shelf. If you pray, you can say a blessing you know. If not, just say thank you, to wherever it came from.

wordCard.voice: Bracha. A blessing, said to the source before you eat, and after you're full. Fifteenth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessing. baruch, blessed, comes from the same root.

carryVoice: Your line: notice before you bite. Two seconds is all the pause asks for. See you tomorrow.
